metadata.summary: The section describes the AGV HMI as a user-friendly application for graphical data presentation and remote control, providing access to management tools such as alarms, position status, speed, and battery levels.

source_refs.quote: AGV HMI is a user-friendly application for graphical data presentation and remote control of the AGV. The application enables to efficiently organize the data and gives the user access to a wide variety of management tools, such as alarms, position status, speed, battery levels and other functions of the AGV.

metadata.summary: The section describes the AGV HMI application as a web-based interface for external devices, requiring connection to the AMR's WiFi network and access via a specific IP address. It lists the main menu elements, including available tasks, the AGV serial number, current mode, network connection status, and battery status.
question_intents: How to access the AGV HMI application

source_refs.quote: The AGV HMI application is dedicated for external devices. To open the application, the operator needs to connect the external device to the AMRs WiFi network and open the following address in the web browser:
192.168.0.100/qursor-hmi (where 192.168.0.100 is the IP address of the AMR).
Main menu with available tasks.

metadata.summary: The HMI control for the AMR Formica is available via a built-in touch-screen or a remote mobile application, with both methods offering similar functionalities that differ primarily in menu access and manual control methods.
question_intents: How is the AGV HMI interface accessed?

source_refs.quote: The HMI control of the AMR Formica can be obtained in two ways - the AGV is equipped with a touch-screen or can be controlled remotely with the AGV HMI application installed on a mobile device. The functionalities of both views are very similar and differ in the way of accessing the main menu and the manual control of the device

metadata.summary: The section describes the layout and functionality of the AGV application's touch-screen interface, including the location of the main menu tabs, the display of the AGV serial number, and the availability of joystick and brake controls within the Manual tab.
question_intents: How to use the AGV touch-screen interface

source_refs.quote: Available main menu of the application is displayed in the form of tabs on the left side of the screen (1)
The serial number of AGV is displayed on the top bar of the application (2)
In Manual tab joystick option is available but the brake control is not possible (3)

metadata.summary: The section describes three AGV operation modes: Automatic, Manual, and Setup, detailing their control methods and intended usage contexts.
question_intents: What are the operation modes of the AGV?

source_refs.quote: AGVs can operate in three different modes. The current mode is displayed in the top bar of the application :
AUTOMATIC MODE - AGV is managed by Qursor M.A.P. system,
MANUAL MODE - AGV is controlled using the touch-screen or remotely by the AGV HMI mobile application on condition that the safety bumper in the AGV is continuously pressed.

metadata.summary: The section explains that AGV modes are changed manually by turning the switch on the main panel to the desired position (manual, setup, or automatic), which automatically updates the mode in the AGV HMI application and displays it in the top bar.
question_intents: How to change AGV modes

source_refs.quote: The modes are changed manually on the main panel of the AGV. Simply turn the switch on the AGV main panel to the desired position (manual, setup or automatic). The new mode will be automatically changed in the AGV HMI application (fig.2) and displayed in the top bar og the application (fig.1).

metadata.summary: The section explains that only one person can control the AGV at a time and describes the process of pressing the Request control button in the Manual control tab to enable operations such as raising/lowering pins and plates, controlling brakes, and steering with a joystick, noting that available operations depend on the HMI control type.
question_intents: How to take control of the AGV

source_refs.quote: Only one person can control the AGV at the same time. To take control of the AGV, press the Request control button (fig.3) in the Manual control tab. Once the manual control is available, the user can raise/lower the pins and plates, control the brakes and steer the AGV with joystick*.
*The types of available operations depend on the type of HMI control (via AGV HMI application or directly on the touch-screen of the AGV. For details refer to AGV-HMI interface)

Speed - current speed of the AGV Position confidence - accuracy of the position relating to the loaded map

title: How to clear the current faults

metadata.summary: The section outlines the procedure for clearing current faults on an AGV, requiring the device to be in manual or setup mode. It instructs the user to verify and remove the fault source, then press the Clear faults button to move the faults to the Historic faults tab, where they are stored for 8 hours.
question_intents: How to clear faults

source_refs.quote: NOTE Faults can be cleared only in manual or setup mode.
Switch the AGV to the manual or setup mode Verify and remove the source of the faults
Press the Clear faults button. The faults will be automatically moved to the Historic faults tab for 8 hours

section_path: Convenient overview and management of current and archive faults
How to clear the current faults

metadata.summary: In Manual or Setup mode, users can control the AGV locally via the AGV HMI application by pressing Request control in the Manual control tab to raise/lower pins and plates and steer using the joystick.

source_refs.quote: In Manual or Setup mode the user can control the AGV locally with the use AGV HMI application. To do so, in Manual control tab press Request control . Here you can raise/lower the pin and plates and steer the AGV using the joystick.

metadata.summary: The AGV detects RFID tags to identify the riser it is approaching. Upon reading, the tag data is verified and registered in the application, including the unique ID of the tag and the type of the riser.

source_refs.quote: AGV can detect RFID tags. This enables to easily identify the raiser, the AGV is approaching to. Once read, the tag data is verified and registered in the application.
Unique ID of the tag
Type of the riser with the tag

title: Non-contact safety sensors for collision avoidance

metadata.summary: The section describes AGV safety sensors that detect obstacles to slow down or stop the vehicle, protecting personnel and preventing mechanical damage. It details two safety fields: a yellow warning zone that triggers a safe speed reduction and a red emergency zone that causes an immediate stop. Additionally, it notes that ultrasonic scanners assist in locating the environment and calculating distance to obstacles.
question_intents: How do non-contact safety sensors function for collision avoidance?

source_refs.quote: AGV safety sensors surround the area and slow down or stop if an obstacle is detected. The sensors can detect people or objects in the path of the AGV, what protects the personnel and helps to avoid the mechanical damage of the AGV.
YELLOW - an obstacle is detected in the warning zone, AGV slows down to the safe speed.
RED - an obstacle is detected in the emergency zone, AGV stops immediately

section_path: Non-contact safety sensors for collision avoidance

metadata.summary: A task is an operation triggered at a station requiring the AGV to perform scheduled activities, with types and configurations defined in a separate Configurator application. The section also lists specific data fields associated with tasks, including trigger time, task name, triggered station, destination, and end time.
question_intents: What is a task?

source_refs.quote: A task is an operation triggered at the station that requires the AGV to perform a sequence of scheduled activities. The type of tasks and their configuration is defined in a separate Configurator application.  In Tasks tab you can overview the currently executed and archive tasks. You can also remove the tasks that are in progress (current tasks). Click on the task to see its details.

metadata.summary: Kanbans are composed of steps containing sequenced jobs with optional preconditions that trigger use cases, and they can be initiated by operators or external systems via the Qursor API.
question_intents: definition

source_refs.quote: Kanbans consist of one or more steps. Each step is a list of jobs to be executed in a specific sequence. Each job is composed of specified preconditions (Conditions) that must be met in order to execute the command (use case)*. After the conditions are met, the use case is triggered, and the system moves on to the next job.

Individual steps are triggered either by operators or by an external system using the Qursor API. After completing a step, which means executing all jobs in its sequence, Qursor waits for the next step to be called.
* It is also possible for a job to have no preconditions.

metadata.summary: The Qursor platform can be installed with an optional Hector connector service that interacts with external traffic systems via REST API or a dummy system. It defines 2D polygon zones, specifically traffic light and lock zones, to control AGV behavior and visualize zone states.
question_intents: What is the Qursor platform and its Hector connector?

source_refs.quote: Qursor platform can be installed with optional Hector connector service. Hector connector has been primarily designed to work with external traffic system by calling its REST API.

We can define a set of zones in the core Qursor configuration. Zones are simply a 2D polygons on the map. Hector connector provides possibility  to  control different zones by different external (or internal/dummy) REST APIs. Qursor fleet management controls behaviour of AGVs depending on the type of zone and Qursor frontend applications visualise the state of the zones.
We distinguish two types of zones: traffic light and lock zones.

metadata.summary: Traffic light zones are used for managing traffic lights, consisting of interdependent yellow and red zones. When an AGV enters the yellow zone, the yellow light activates; upon entering the associated red zone, the yellow light turns off and the red light turns on.
question_intents: How do traffic light zones function?

source_refs.quote: Traffic light zones are used for traffic lights management. Two types of traffic lights can be set:

Zone types are interdependent. When the AGV enters the yellow zone, it lights up yellow, when it enters the associated red zone, the yellow light goes off and the red light comes on. An example of the sequence of lighting zones is shown in the pictures below.

metadata.summary: Lock zones are used for traffic management to separate areas accessible to AGVs from those for unmanaged vehicles. When free, AGVs can enter and block unmanaged vehicles; when locked by an external vehicle, the zone turns grey and displays blocking and waiting vehicle names. The next vehicle in the queue can lock the zone upon release. Forceful release of external locks or manual bypass of permissions is possible but not recommended due to collision risks.

When the zone is locked by external vehicle it turns grey. Information about the lock is shown after clicking on the zone area.
The lock can be forcefully released in Qursor even when it is external lock. This action is not recommended; it can lead to collisions. Use only when needed.

metadata.summary: The section describes the mapping of zone IDs created in Qursor Configurator to zoneIDs in the Navithor map via the Qursor Fleet Manager configuration file (zones.json). It details the structure of the zones, locks, and relations sections, explaining how AGV tags lock zones and how logical operations on zoneID points determine zone locking conditions.
question_intents: How are zones mapped between Qursor Configurator and Navithor?

source_refs.quote: All zones ID created in Qursor Configurator must be mapped with zoneID in Navithor map. This is done in the Qursor Fleet Manager configuration file - zones.json . Zones have assigned areas - groups of points that trigger a request to block the zone when AGV meets them.

 zones section - links zoneID points from Navithor Tools map with zone created in Qursor Configurator. Configurator zone ID is defined as id and Navithor zoneID is defined in areas. areas condition is checked based on logical operations: [zoneID1 AND zoneID2] OR [zoneID3]. Zone is locked when AGV goes through segments with zoneID1 and zoneID2 (in ony order) or with zoneID3.
 locks section - defines AGV tags used for locking zones. AGV tag is a combination of prefix and lock. For example, AGV 1201 will lock zone with tag agv_1201.

metadata.summary: The section warns that placing zone IDs on the map is sensitive and that modifying the map or changing IDs may disturb the operation of zones in Qursor.
question_intents: What are the limitations regarding zone ID placement?

source_refs.quote:  Placing zone IDs on the map is very sensitive. With any modification of the map, it is important to keep this in mind, because any changes in the ID may disturb the operation of zones in Qursor.
